opus-5.5.text:
I think the basic promise is pretty clear if you look at how the current paradigm actually works. Reinforcement learning on its own is extremely sample inefficient when you start from nothing. If you just drop a randomly initialized agent into a complex environment and wait for it to stumble onto reward, you could be waiting essentially forever, because the space of possible behaviors is so vast and the reward is so sparse. What pretraining on human data does is give you a prior that's already in the right neighborhood. The model has absorbed an enormous amount of information about how people reason, write code, solve math problems, and so on, so when you then apply RL, you're not searching blindly. You're refining behavior that's already somewhat competent, and the reward signal actually has something to latch onto.

You can see this in the recent reasoning models. The RL that goes into them is working on top of a base model that already "knows" a lot, and the RL is mostly eliciting and sharpening capabilities rather than creating them from scratch. That's a big reason it works as well as it does with relatively modest amounts of RL compute compared to pretraining.

The limitation, I think, has a few parts. One is that human data is skewed toward what humans happen to write down, which isn't the same as what you need to be competent at a task. A lot of the most important knowledge for, say, running a company, doing a scientific research project, or operating in the physical world, is tacit. People don't produce long transcripts of themselves carefully reasoning through every decision over months. So the internet is very rich in some areas, like short-horizon text tasks or competition math, and very thin in others, like long-horizon agency, coordination, and dealing with messy real-world feedback. If your prior is weak in those areas, RL doesn't have a good starting point, and you're back toward the sparse reward problem.

The second limitation is about horizon length and verifiability. RL works best when you can cheaply check whether an outcome was good. For math and coding, you often can. For many economically valuable tasks, the feedback is delayed, noisy, and expensive to obtain. Human data can help you get a policy that looks reasonable, but turning that into something reliably good over long horizons requires a lot of feedback that's hard to generate at scale.

And then there's the question of whether you can go beyond human level at all. Imitation by itself sort of caps you at the distribution you're imitating. RL is the thing that in principle lets you exceed it, as with AlphaGo or AlphaZero. But that worked because Go has a perfect simulator and a clean reward. In most real domains you don't have that, so the extent to which you can bootstrap past human performance depends heavily on building good environments and good verifiers, which is a lot of slow, unglamorous work.

So my overall view is that human data is an incredibly valuable bootstrap, and it's probably why progress has been as fast as it has been. But I don't think it automatically gets you to the capabilities that matter most for broad automation. The bottleneck shifts toward things like constructing rich environments, gathering data on long-horizon tasks, and getting feedback from the real world, and those things scale more slowly than just throwing more compute at pretraining. That's one of the reasons I tend to expect the transition to be more gradual than some people think.

r001.rationale: The response says human-data pretraining gives RL a useful prior, so it refines already competent behavior instead of searching blindly when rewards are sparse.

r002.rationale: It distinguishes what people write down from tacit knowledge and notes that people rarely produce transcripts of their reasoning through decisions, raising the gap between observable records and internal cognition.

r003.rationale: The response says RL can exceed human performance in principle and cites AlphaGo, but it does not reject the inference that RL cannot work merely because it has not yet been demonstrated for a capability.

fable-5.1.text:
Right, so I think the promise is fairly straightforward, and the limitation is a bit more subtle. The promise is that human data gives you a starting point. If you try to do reinforcement learning from scratch on something like writing a correct piece of software or proving a theorem, the problem is that the reward is extremely sparse. A randomly initialized policy will essentially never succeed, so you never get a gradient signal, and you're stuck. What pretraining on human data does is it puts you in a regime where the model already succeeds some reasonable fraction of the time, maybe one percent, maybe ten percent, and that's enough to get the RL process off the ground. You can then amplify that, do rejection sampling, train on the successful trajectories, and bootstrap your way up. So in that sense, human data is a very good prior, and I think a lot of the progress we've seen over the past couple of years is really this story. You have a strong prior from pretraining, and then you use RL to sharpen it in domains where you have verifiable rewards.

The limitation is that this works best precisely in the domains where humans have already produced a lot of relevant data and where you can check answers. Math and coding are the obvious cases. There's a huge amount of text about them, and you can verify a proof or run a test suite. But the capabilities people actually care about for transforming the economy are often not like that. Think about running a research program over several months, or managing a project, or doing experimental work where the feedback loop is slow and noisy. Humans don't write down the process they go through very much. There's a lot of tacit knowledge that never ends up in the training distribution. And so the prior you get from human data for those tasks is quite weak, and at the same time you don't have a clean reward signal to do RL against. So you're hit on both sides.

There's also a more conceptual worry, which is that if you bootstrap from human data, you might inherit the structure of how humans solve problems, and that structure is not necessarily optimal for the system you're training. It's a bit like how AlphaGo was initially bootstrapped from human games and then AlphaZero did better by throwing that away entirely. Now, Go is a domain where self-play works because the environment is cheap and the reward is perfect, and I don't think we can just copy that recipe for most real-world tasks. But it does suggest that the human prior is a crutch you eventually want to remove, and the question is whether you can remove it before you run out of the easy gains.

So my overall view would be that human data is what makes current RL approaches feasible at all, and we should expect continued progress in the domains that are well-covered by it. But I'd be cautious about extrapolating from the pace in math and coding to the much broader set of capabilities that would be needed for something like a large acceleration in economic growth. For those, I think the bottleneck is less about the training algorithm and more about where the signal is going to come from, and I don't think we have a convincing answer to that yet.

r001.rationale: It says human pretraining gives the model a starting level of competence, allowing RL to get a signal despite sparse rewards.

r002.rationale: It points to humans’ undocumented problem-solving processes and tacit knowledge as information missing from training data, raising the need for data about internal human processes.

r003.rationale: It says there is no convincing answer to where training signal will come from for broader tasks, but does not reject the inference that RL cannot work because it has not yet been shown to work for a capability.

astra-6.text:
Human data can give you a very useful starting point. If you train a model on demonstrations of people doing a task, you don’t have to discover everything through trial and error. The model already has some sense of what a reasonable approach looks like, and reinforcement learning can then improve on that.

But there’s a distinction between learning to imitate a successful solution and learning to find one. You might have a mathematical proof that took someone months to produce, and the published proof doesn’t show all the failed attempts or the decisions that led them there. So the data gives you the final product, but only a limited picture of the process you want the model to learn.

Reinforcement learning could fill that gap if you can reliably evaluate the model’s attempts and give it enough opportunities to explore. The difficulty is that, for some tasks, success is so rare that even a model trained on human examples won’t find it often enough to learn much. Or evaluating success is itself expensive or ambiguous.

So I wouldn’t think of human performance as a ceiling. You can potentially start with human data and go beyond it. But having good human examples doesn’t automatically give you an efficient path to much stronger capabilities. That depends on whether the examples put you within reach of useful exploration, and whether you have a feedback signal that actually rewards progress.

r001.rationale: It describes human demonstrations as a useful starting point that gives the model a reasonable approach for reinforcement learning to improve, while noting that sparse success can make learning difficult.

r002.rationale: It contrasts the final product in human examples with the missing failed attempts, decisions, and process that produced it, raising the need for data about human problem-solving.

r003.rationale: It says models may go beyond human performance, but does not address the inference that reinforcement learning cannot work because nobody has already made it work.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the promise is that human data gives you a very good starting point. If you’re trying to train a system to solve difficult problems, having it learn from human solutions can get it to the point where reinforcement learning starts being productive. It already knows something about what a sensible approach looks like, so it doesn’t have to discover everything by trial and error.

But there’s a distinction between providing a starting point and providing a signal for further improvement. If you have problems where you can reliably check the answer, then the system can potentially go beyond the humans who supplied the training data. You don’t need a human to demonstrate every better solution; you need a way to recognize that it’s better.

The limitation becomes more serious when evaluating the output is itself difficult. If your feedback comes from human judgments, and the system is doing something humans don’t really understand, then those judgments may stop tracking actual performance. You might end up training it to produce things that look convincing rather than things that are correct.

So I wouldn’t think of human data as necessarily setting a ceiling on capability. It can be a way to bootstrap a process that goes much further. The question is whether, once you leave the range where humans can provide good demonstrations, you still have a reliable learning signal.

r001.rationale: The response says human solutions can give a system a starting point that makes reinforcement learning productive, but it does not mention sparse rewards.

r002.rationale: The response discusses human solutions and human judgments, but does not raise the possibility that training data could concern internal human cognition.

r003.rationale: The response says human data need not cap capability, but does not reject the claim that reinforcement learning cannot work merely because nobody has made it work before.
